lesson.grammar_point: cohesive devices: addition linkers and this or these with a summary noun

listenings.text: I edit a law journal, and I read papers from all over the world. The ideas are usually excellent. The most common problem is not grammar. It is sentences that are too long. A reader in English expects one idea per sentence and one main idea per paragraph. My second piece of advice is about the word this. Many authors start a sentence with this, alone, and the reader does not know what it refers to. This decision, this approach, this problem: add the noun, and the reader never gets lost. Finally, read your text out loud. If you need to breathe in the middle of a sentence, the sentence is too long.

When I arrived in New York, I wrote like a Brazilian judge. Some of my sentences were eighty words long, with three or four ideas inside. I thought that was elegant. My first memo came back from my partner with one comment, in red: too long, where is the takeaway? I was a bit offended. But she was right. American clients read on their phones, between meetings. Now my rule is simple. The takeaway goes in the first sentence. Each sentence has one idea. And I connect them with small words: this, moreover, in addition. My memos are shorter now, and clients actually answer them.

How do busy professionals read their email? A communication company studied the inboxes of two thousand office workers, and the answer is: very fast. The average professional receives more than one hundred emails a day. Most people read only the subject line and the first sentence before they decide to open an email or not. Emails with long paragraphs are much less likely to get an answer. The researchers' advice is simple. Put the main point in the subject line, use short sentences and bullet points, and proofread before you send. Your reader is busy, and the first ten seconds decide everything.
